analysis.one_liner: Requires power plants to modernize, sharply cut mercury and other pollution, and pay a fee on carbon emissions.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Finance Committee: it was introduced in October 1998 with no cosponsors and died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999 without any vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every fossil fuel power plant in the country — including the old 'grandfathered' plants that escape strict Clean Air Act rules — to meet modern efficiency and emission standards within ten years. Plants would have to remove 95% of mercury, cut sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides by 90-95%, and pay a gradually phased-in federal fee of up to $50 per ton of carbon dioxide. To ease the burden, it offered tax breaks to utilities that build cleaner plants, grants to publicly owned utilities, retraining money for coal workers, and development aid for coal communities, funded by the carbon fees.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who breathes air downwind of old coal and oil plants, people who eat fish contaminated with mercury (especially pregnant women and children), and ratepayers, since burning fuel at 45-50% efficiency instead of the national average of 33% wastes far less fuel. Renewable energy industries (solar, wind, biomass, geothermal) get tax credits and demonstration funding, and coal workers and towns get retraining and economic development money.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Downwind communities, fish consumers, renewable energy

how_it_helps.text: Ends the 'grandfather' loophole: all fossil plants, regardless of age, must comply with the strict new source review standards that only 23% of the 1,000 largest emitting units faced in 1998 [S2][S3].

Requires coal and oil plants to remove 95% of mercury, a neurotoxin that the bill's findings say especially threatens pregnant women, fetuses, and children, and whose fish-consumption advisories had risen 86% between 1993 and 1996 [S3].

Sets emission limits on carbon dioxide, sulfur dioxide, and nitrogen oxides, and requires plants to raise combustion efficiency from the then-average 33% to 45% (existing plants) or 50% (new plants) [S2][S3].

Imposes a carbon fee of $50 per ton of CO2, phased in from 2003 to 2009, deposited into a Clean Air Trust Fund that pays for modernization grants, coal worker retraining, and coal community development [S3].

Provides $75 million per year for coal worker retraining and $75 million per year for economic development in coal-dependent communities, explicitly cushioning the people the cleanup would hurt most [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Owners of old, inefficient coal- and oil-fired plants, which would face steep modernization costs or forced retirement, plus a $50-per-ton carbon fee. Coal mining companies would face reduced demand. Some of these costs would likely pass through to electricity customers in coal-reliant regions, which is why the bill includes transition aid for workers and communities.
analysis.who_pays_short: Coal plant owners and the coal industry

drawbacks.text: The $50-per-ton carbon fee would raise generation costs, and plant owners would likely pass much of that through to electricity customers, particularly in coal-dependent regions [S3].

Forcing every plant to a 45% efficiency standard within ten years is a demanding deadline for utilities with large fleets of 1960s-era units, and the bill's own tax breaks and grants to help them comply add federal cost; critics would call the timetable and the subsidy package heavy-handed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health and environmental stakes were large — the bill's findings cite pollution linked to roughly 50,000 deaths a year and widespread mercury contamination — and the bill tried to blunt the main cost by funding worker retraining and community aid from the carbon fees themselves. The costs to plant owners and coal regions are real, and the ten-year compliance clock was aggressive, but the design directly offsets the harm it would cause.

outcome.mechanism: Leahy introduced it in mid-October 1998, just weeks before the 105th Congress ended; the Senate referred it to the Finance Committee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the Congress expired.

narrative.text: Leahy introduced the bill on October 15, 1998 and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance [S5][S1].
No other senator cosponsored the bill [S4].
The Finance Committee took no further action, and the Congress ended on January 3, 1999 without the bill ever reaching the floor [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Owners of old, grandfathered coal-fired power plants and the coal industry benefited from the bill's death: they continued operating pre-1970 plants under far looser rules, with no efficiency mandate, no mercury requirement, and no carbon fee.

for.name: Sen. Patrick Leahy
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate; no other senator joined as a cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill attracted no cosponsors of either party and never reached a vote, so no roll-call or bipartisan pattern exists to measure.

industries.note: The bill forces their aging plants to meet strict efficiency and emission standards and pay up to $50 per ton of carbon dioxide, threatening wholesale replacement of grandfathered fleets. Their low-cost, high-pollution business model depends on the loophole the bill closes.
Efficiency mandates and a carbon fee would cut coal demand by electric generators; the bill even budgets aid for coal workers and towns displaced by reduced coal consumption.

industries.industry: Investor-owned utilities building new efficient plants
industries.note: The same bill gives compliant investor-owned units accelerated depreciation and gives publicly owned utilities matching grants, so the utilities that modernize are compensated with tax dollars — public money routed through the industry to pay for its own cleanup.

industries.industry: Solar, wind, biomass, and geothermal energy
industries.note: The bill extends the renewable production tax credit to solar and funds $75 million a year in demonstration projects for biomass, geothermal, solar, and wind generation.
